modules.name: Align
modules.header:
Applying a spec's width, fill and alignment to text that is already rendered.
Padding is the one part of a spec every type applies the same way, so it is written once: measure the rendering,
and if the width asks for more columns, write fill where the alignment says. It lives here rather than with the
numeric conversion engine because it is a text operation — it counts scalars and writes fill bytes, and knows
nothing about digits — which is what lets Time, Uuid and Path align their output without depending on Format.
Zero-padding is deliberately not here. Its zeros go inside the number, between the sign and the digits, so
`-7` at width four is `-007` rather than `00-7`. That is a fact about how a number is spelled, so the numeric
writer owns it.

modules.name: BufferWriter
modules.header:
A fixed buffer that holds text, and holds it at every moment.
`Rux/Format`'s `ByteCursor` is the other fixed-buffer destination and answers a different question. It is
conversion machinery: a number's digits go into it and it never asks whether they are text, because the code
putting them there already knows. It also keeps whatever fitted when a write overruns, since the partial content
is the caller's own buffer and is visible through `Written`.
This one is for text a caller does not vouch for. Every write is validated as UTF-8 before any of it lands, and a
write that does not fit lands not at all. That second promise is what makes the buffer usable after a failure: a
caller who runs out of room can write somewhere larger without first working out how much of the last run went in
and undoing it. `Written` is therefore always exactly the runs that succeeded, in order, and always valid UTF-8.
Neither promise costs a copy. Validation reads the run in place, and the fit is decided by comparing two lengths;
bytes move once, after both have passed.

modules.name: CString
modules.header:
Crossing the boundary to C, where a string is a pointer and a promise.
A C string carries no length: it ends at the first zero byte, and the byte itself is not part of the text. That
convention meets Rux text at exactly two edges, and both need a check nothing else in this package needs.
Going out, the text must not contain a zero byte. One in the middle would silently truncate whatever C does with
the pointer — a path that opens the wrong file, a query that drops its tail — so a string holding one is
refused, not truncated. Truncation is the attack, not the accident: text that reads one way to a checker reading
lengths and another way to a C API reading terminators is how "safe.txt\0.exe" gets past a filter.
Coming in, the terminator is how far to read, and the bytes must still be UTF-8: nothing about C promises text,
so bytes from C are input, and input is validated.
Nothing here weakens what `String` promises. A `CString` is its own type owning its own copy, so the NUL it
appends is never visible through anything else, and a `String` never holds one.

modules.name: Display
modules.header:
The two ways a value turns into text.
`Display` is the text a value has for a reader: a number is its digits, a string is its characters, and nothing is
quoted or escaped. `Debug` is the text a value has for whoever is looking at a program: a string is quoted with
its escapes visible, a character is quoted, and a structure shows its parts. They differ for exactly the types
where the difference matters, and a type with only one sensible rendering implements both the same way.
Both write into a `TextWriter` rather than answering with a `String`, which is what makes printing a value
allocate nothing. Rendering to a string is then one writer among several.
Both take the placeholder's specification, because it is the value that has to apply it: base and sign need the
bits and not the rendered text, and precision means digits to a float and characters to a string. What every
type applies the same way — width, fill, alignment — is written once in `WriteAligned` and shared. A bare `{}`
passes `FormatSpec::Plain`, which asks for nothing.
These contracts live in Text rather than in Format so that a package can describe its own values without
depending on the numeric conversion engine. Time, Uuid and Path all implement them and none of them needs to
know how a float is rounded.

modules.name: ErrorPresentation
modules.header:
What an error looks like when a program has to say what went wrong.
Two renderings, and the split is the same one `Display` and `Debug` have everywhere else, applied to the case
where it matters most. `Display` is the description a reader is shown — a short phrase that fits inside a
sentence a program is already writing, such as "could not read the file: out of memory". `Debug` names the case
itself, with whatever payload it carries: `FormatError::InvalidSpecification(12)`. One is for the person the
program is talking to; the other is for the person reading a log.
The descriptions are stable. That is a promise worth making explicitly, because an error description ends up in
somebody's log, somebody's issue report and eventually somebody's grep, and changing the words later breaks all
three quietly. What is not promised is that a description is a parsing contract: it says what happened, and the
case name is what a program should branch on.
This file presents the low-level errors this package already depends on — `AllocError` from Allocator and
`PageError` from Memory — because they surface through `TextError` and a caller holding one should not have to
write the words itself. Those are the only foreign types here. In particular `EntropyError` is deliberately
absent and has no `Display` or `Debug` in v0.1.0: presenting it would require an edge between Entropy and either
this package or Format, and the layering forbids both. A caller holding an `EntropyError` handles its cases or
wraps it in a diagnostic type of its own.

modules.name: FormatError
modules.header:
Why a value could not be turned into text.
`TextError` next door answers a different question: why storing or validating text failed. Both are failure-only.
Every case denotes a failure, there is no `None`, `Ok` or `Success` case, and success lives exclusively in the
other channel of the native fallible an operation returns. `TextFailureKind` carries the ways text handling fails
when one of them surfaces through formatting.
The categories are split by who is at fault, because that is what a caller can act on. A malformed specification
or an argument-count mismatch is the call site's mistake and carries where. An unsupported request or a value out
of range is a mismatch between a value and what was asked of it. Insufficient capacity is the destination being
too small. A writer failure is the destination itself failing, and its details stay in the adapter that knows
them: this package has no vocabulary for a broken pipe and does not pretend to.

modules.name: Presentation
modules.header:
Text rendering itself is the text it already is.
A `String` and a `StringView` write their bytes straight through, with no conversion: they are UTF-8 by
construction, which is exactly what a writer takes. Nothing is copied and nothing is allocated, which is the
difference from the old shape, where rendering a string produced a second string.
`Debug` is where the two part company. A string shown to a reader is its characters; a string shown to somebody
looking at a program is quoted and escaped, so that where it starts and stops is visible, an empty one is not
invisible, and a newline or a tab reads as what it is rather than moving the cursor.
What is escaped is deliberately narrow: the quote and the backslash, because they would otherwise be ambiguous
with the quoting itself, and the C0 and C1 controls, because they do something to a terminal instead of being
read. Everything else stays as it is. Escaping every non-ASCII character would make text in most of the world's
scripts unreadable in exactly the place a reader is trying to read it, and it is text — the fact that it survives
a round trip through a terminal is the whole point of it being UTF-8.

modules.name: Search
modules.header:
Looking through text without copying any of it.
Everything here answers about a `StringView` and gives back views, positions or booleans — never a new string.
That is the point: asking whether text starts with something, or where something occurs in it, or what it is
without its surrounding spaces, are all questions about bytes that already exist. A design that answered with
owning strings would allocate to answer a question, and a caller who only wanted to look would pay for a copy.
The search is over bytes, and works out to a search over characters for free: UTF-8 is self-synchronising, so no
character's encoding is a suffix of another's and no byte of a multi-byte character can be mistaken for the start
of one. A match on bytes therefore always lands on a character boundary, and there is nothing extra to check.
Case is not considered anywhere here. Two characters differing only in case are the same letter to a reader and
different bytes to a machine, and which pairs count is a Unicode question with a locale attached. `Transform` has
the ASCII-only answer, which is the one that is well defined without tables.

modules.name: Spec
modules.header:
What a placeholder may ask for, parsed once and handed to the value.
The grammar inside `{}` after the colon is `[[fill]align][sign][#][0][width][.precision][base]`, each piece
optional: `{:>8}` right-aligns in eight columns, `{:+}` shows a positive sign, `{:08x}` zero-pads eight hex
digits, `{:#b}` prefixes binary with `0b`, `{:.3}` keeps three characters of text, `{:.2e}` writes a float in
scientific notation with two digits after the point. The spec belongs to the
placeholder and not to the value — the same value renders differently under different placeholders — but it is
the value that applies it, because base and sign need the bits and not the rendered text.
The representation is private and read through accessors. That is not ceremony: a spec is what a placeholder
asked for, and a value applying one must not be able to change it. Before this moved packages the fields were
reachable by anything in Format, and moving it here would otherwise have handed the same reach to every package
that renders a value. Reading is what implementations need; writing belongs to the parser alone.

modules.name: String
modules.header:
Text that owns the bytes it holds.
A `String` owns one block, knows the allocator to give it back to, and never writes to it again. Every operation
that produces different text produces a different `String`, and leaves the receiver as it was.
Immutability is not a preference here, it is what makes the type safe to hand around: a `String` may be built over
bytes that came from a literal, and a literal lives on a read-only page. A type that promised mutation would have
to copy defensively on every write or fault on some of them. `StringBuilder` is where text is assembled; `String`
is what assembling it produces.
Copying makes an independent block from the same allocator, so strings have value semantics even though each owns
storage. A fallible caller can use `Clone`; the language copy operation cannot return an error and therefore
terminates if its allocation fails. `StringView` borrows and copies no bytes; `View` creates one for free.
Every `String` this package produces holds well-formed UTF-8, checked once where the bytes enter. Everything
downstream may rely on that, which is what makes cutting and indexing cheap.

modules.name: StringBuilder
modules.header:
Where text is assembled.
A `String` is immutable, so building one a piece at a time through `String` alone would allocate and copy on every
step — quadratic work to produce a linear result. A builder keeps spare room and doubles it, so a sequence of
appends costs each byte a constant amount on average, and hands the block over at the end without copying it.
The builder holds well-formed UTF-8 at every moment, not only at the end. That is why it accepts whole characters
and checked runs of bytes rather than arbitrary ones: a builder that could hold half a character would make
`View` a lie and `IntoString` a validation pass. Appending an incomplete sequence is refused rather than deferred.
It prohibits copying and `~StringBuilder` gives its block back. `IntoString` transfers the block without copying;
after it the builder owns nothing and is ready to be used again.

modules.name: StringView
modules.header:
A borrowed run of text that is known to be UTF-8.
The point of a separate type is that the check happens once. A `char8[..]` may or may not be UTF-8, so every
function taking one either re-validates — which turns a linear pass into a linear pass per call — or assumes,
which is where the bugs are. A `StringView` cannot be built without the bytes being checked, so everything
downstream may assume and be right.
It borrows: making one copies no bytes and owns nothing, so it is `Copy` and has no destructor. The bytes must
outlive it, and nothing here tracks that. `String` is what owns bytes.
Every index it takes and gives is a byte index, not a scalar index. Counting scalars is linear, so an interface
in scalar indices would make indexing linear without saying so; byte indices are constant, and a cut at one that
is not a boundary is rejected rather than splitting a character in half.

modules.name: Structure
modules.header:
Showing what is inside an outcome or a sequence, without taking it apart.
An optional, a fallible and a slice are the three shapes almost every diagnostic is written around, and none of
them can implement `Debug` on its own: what a `T?` looks like depends entirely on what `T` looks like, and native
forms implement no interface at all. So these are handwritten functions with the bound written out —
`WriteOptionalDebug<T: Debug>` — which is the shape the language does have. Each instantiation
resolves its element's `WriteDebug` at compile time; nothing is dispatched at run time and nothing is reflected
over.
The whole point is that they borrow. `??` and `?` consume the optional, because taking a payload out is a transfer
of ownership. But showing a value is not taking it: a `match` on a borrowed optional binds its payload where it
lies, and that binding is what these hand to the element's `WriteDebug`.
So an option holding a move-only value can be written twice and still hold it, which is the only behaviour worth
having — a diagnostic that consumed what it printed would be a diagnostic nobody could put in front of a value
they still needed.
The specification describes the *elements*, not the container. There is no numeric or textual form a sequence
has of its own for a width or a precision to apply to, so each element is handed the caller's specification
unchanged and does with it whatever that element type does — `{:x}` over a slice of integers writes each one in
hexadecimal. The brackets, the commas and the case names are punctuation and are never padded, so a specification
that an element ignores changes nothing at all.
Sequential containers are in `Rux/Collections`, which borrows a run of elements out of a vector, an array or a
deque and calls `WriteSliceDebug` with it. Nothing here knows those types exist.

modules.name: TextError
modules.header:
What can go wrong in this package, and nothing else.
Two things can, and they are different in kind. An allocation can fail, which says nothing about the text and
everything about the machine; and bytes can fail to be UTF-8, which says nothing about the machine and everything
about where the bytes came from. A caller handles those differently — one is retried or reported, the other means
the input is not text — so they are not one error.

modules.name: Transform
modules.header:
Making new text out of old.
Everything here allocates, because everything here produces text that did not exist before: joining two runs,
repeating one, replacing part of one, changing the case of one. That is what separates these from `Search`, whose
answers are all borrows of what was already there.
The case operations are ASCII-only and say so in their names. Case in Unicode is not a per-character mapping: it
depends on the locale (a Turkish dotless i), on neighbours (a Greek final sigma), and it changes the length (a
German sharp s becomes two letters). Every one of those needs the tables, and a `ToUpper` that quietly did the
ASCII thing to text that was not ASCII would be wrong in a way nobody notices until the text is not English.

modules.name: Utf8
modules.header:
UTF-8, decoded and encoded by the table that defines it.
A byte sequence is well-formed UTF-8 only if it matches Table 3-7 of the Unicode standard, and that table is not
the obvious one. The obvious rule — read the leading byte for a length, then take that many continuation bytes --
accepts three things the standard rejects, and each of them has been a security hole in something:
- **Overlong forms.** `C0 80` would decode to U+0000 under the obvious rule. Encoding one scalar two ways means a
  check that looks for a byte sequence can be walked around by spelling it differently.
- **Surrogate halves.** U+D800 through U+DFFF are not scalar values; they exist only as a UTF-16 encoding
  mechanism. Encoded in UTF-8 they are `ED A0 80` and up, and accepting them lets text carry values that cannot
  round-trip through UTF-16.
- **Values past U+10FFFF.** Four bytes can express up to U+1FFFFF; Unicode stops at U+10FFFF.
The table forbids all three by constraining the *second* byte's range per leading byte, rather than by decoding
and checking afterwards. That is what the ranges below are: a leading byte of `E0` admits only `A0..BF` next,
which is exactly the set that cannot produce an overlong; `ED` admits only `80..9F`, which is exactly the set
that cannot produce a surrogate. Checking after the fact would work too, and is easier to get subtly wrong.
Every function here works on borrowed bytes and allocates nothing.

modules.name: Writer
modules.header:
Where formatted text goes.
Formatting used to answer with a `String`, which meant every value rendered allocated a block, had its bytes
copied somewhere else, and released the block again. Printing a line of six values allocated six times to produce
text that went straight to a file descriptor.
A writer is the other way round: a value writes its bytes into whatever the caller supplies, and what that is —
a builder, a file, a fixed buffer — is the caller's business. Rendering a value into a string is then one
particular writer rather than the only shape available, and printing one allocates nothing at all.
What is written must be well-formed UTF-8 and must not stop part-way through a character. Every writer relies on
that; a builder's promise that it holds text at every moment is exactly this promise passed along.
A writer's permitted failures are deliberately narrow, and the narrowness is the contract. Only the destination
can say it is full, that its backing text failed, or that it failed on its own terms. A malformed specification,
an unsupported request, an argument-count mismatch and a value out of range all belong to the parser, the value
or the placeholder engine, so a writer that invented one would be reporting a fault it cannot have observed.

that cannot land is not worth reading.
These are the only two failures this writer produces. There is no destination beyond the buffer, so a

arithmetic, neither of which a fixed buffer performs.

doc.summary: Parses the text between `{:` and `}`.
doc.markdown:
Parses the text between `{:` and `}`.
The grammar is `[[fill]align][+][#][0][width][.precision][style]`, every piece optional, so the empty
specification is well-formed and asks for nothing. A style is an identifier: an ASCII letter followed by
letters, digits, `_` or `-`. That covers the single-letter integer bases `b`, `o`, `x` and `X`, which also set
`Base` so an integer need not inspect the style text, the float styles `e` and `E` for scientific notation, and
the domain styles such as `iso8601` and `hyphenated` that a value interprets for itself.
Syntax is recognized here once; whether a style or flag *applies* is the value's question, since only the value
knows whether a precision means digits, characters or nothing at all. A specification this accepts may still be
refused with `UnsupportedRequest` by the value it is handed to.
The returned specification's style borrows `text`. It must not outlive the specification text it was parsed
from, and nothing here tracks that.
Reports `InvalidSpecification` carrying the zero-based byte offset into `text` where parsing stopped: an
unprintable or brace fill, a `.` with no digits after it, a width or precision whose arithmetic will not fit a
`uint`, or any byte that can begin none of the remaining pieces. Nothing is written and no partial
specification escapes.

doc.summary: Refuses a specification that names any style.
doc.markdown:
Refuses a specification that names any style.
The parser recognizes a style wherever the grammar allows one; whether it *means* anything is the value's
question. A value with no styles of its own calls this so that `{:q}` is refused rather than silently rendered
as though nothing had been asked for.
Reports `UnsupportedRequest` when a style was written.
doc.returns: success when no style was named

doc.summary: Refuses a specification whose style is not one of the integer bases.
doc.markdown:
Refuses a specification whose style is not one of the integer bases.
What an integer supports is exactly `b`, `o`, `x` and `X`, and each of those is already reflected in `Base`.
So a style that left the base decimal is one this value has no meaning for, which is what this refuses. It is
the integer counterpart of `RejectStyle` and exists for the same reason.
Reports `UnsupportedRequest` for a style that names no base.
doc.returns: success when no style was named, or the style named a base

doc.summary: Decodes the scalar value starting at `index`, reporting it and how many bytes it occupied.
doc.markdown:
Decodes the scalar value starting at `index`, reporting it and how many bytes it occupied.
`bytes` is borrowed. On a failure the caller decides what to do — a decoder replacing bad input with U+FFFD
advances one byte and carries on, and one rejecting it stops.
Cannot allocate. Runs in constant time.
doc.returns: the scalar and its width, or why the bytes there are not one

doc.summary: Whether `bytes` is well-formed UTF-8 from end to end, reporting where it first is not.
doc.markdown:
Whether `bytes` is well-formed UTF-8 from end to end, reporting where it first is not.
`bytes` is borrowed. A failure carries the index of the byte that starts the offending sequence.
Cannot allocate. Runs in time proportional to the length.
doc.returns: nothing when every byte is part of a valid sequence, or where and why the first one is not

items.name: IsBoundary
items.signature: pub func IsBoundary(bytes: char8[..], index: uint) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether `index` is where a scalar value starts, and so a place a string may be cut.
doc.markdown:
Whether `index` is where a scalar value starts, and so a place a string may be cut.
The length counts as a boundary, so the end of a string is always a legal cut. An index past the length is not.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: whether `index` falls between two scalar values rather than inside one

doc.summary: How many scalar values `bytes` holds, assuming it is well-formed.
doc.markdown:
How many scalar values `bytes` holds, assuming it is well-formed.
Counts leading bytes, which is one per scalar value in well-formed UTF-8. Bytes that are not well-formed give a
count that means nothing; `Validate` is what answers whether they are.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: how many scalar values the bytes encode

items.name: BoundaryAtOrBelow
items.signature: pub func BoundaryAtOrBelow(bytes: char8[..], index: uint) -> uint

doc.summary: The index of the scalar boundary at or below `index`.
doc.markdown:
The index of the scalar boundary at or below `index`.
An index inside a sequence is walked back to the start of that sequence, which is what a caller cutting at an
arbitrary byte offset needs. An index at or past the length gives the length.
doc.returns: the largest boundary at or below `index`, so a truncation splits nothing

doc.summary: Somewhere formatted text can be written.
doc.markdown:
Somewhere formatted text can be written.
Writing advances the writer, so `Write` borrows its receiver mutably and is called through a `&var TextWriter`
view, which refers to the caller's own writer rather than a copy that would lose its position.

members.name: Write
members.signature: func Write(self: &var Self, bytes: char8[..]) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: Writes `bytes`, which must be well-formed UTF-8 and must not end part-way through a character.
doc.markdown:
Writes `bytes`, which must be well-formed UTF-8 and must not end part-way through a character.
A successful write accepted the complete run: there is no partial success to report, and a caller may write
the next run without asking how much of this one landed.
May return only `InsufficientCapacity`, `TextFailure` or `WriterFailure`. An implementation must not
originate `InvalidSpecification`, `UnsupportedRequest`, `ArgumentCountMismatch` or `ValueOutOfRange`, none of
which a destination is in a position to observe. Whether anything was written before a failure is the
implementation's own documented guarantee: a bounded buffer leaves itself unchanged, while a stream may
already have emitted a prefix.

params.name: bytes
params.markdown: the UTF-8 run to write, whole

doc.returns: success when the complete run was accepted

items.name: WriteBytes
items.signature: pub func WriteBytes(writer: &var TextWriter, bytes: char8[..]) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: Writes `bytes` to `writer`.
doc.markdown:
Writes `bytes` to `writer`.
The writer is borrowed exclusively for the call, so position changes remain visible to its owner. This forwards
without inspecting the bytes, which is what keeps the writer's permitted failures exactly the writer's.

params.name: bytes
params.markdown: the UTF-8 run to write, whole

doc.returns: whatever the writer reported

items.name: WriteAscii
items.signature: pub func WriteAscii(writer: &var TextWriter, byte: char8) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: Writes one ASCII byte.
doc.markdown:
Writes one ASCII byte.
Reports `TextFailure(InvalidUtf8)` for a byte above 0x7F: a single byte above that is never a whole character,
and a writer takes whole characters. `WriteScalar` is what writes one that needs more than a byte. Otherwise
reports whatever the writer reported.
doc.returns: success when the byte was accepted

items.name: WriteScalar
items.signature: pub func WriteScalar(writer: &var TextWriter, scalar: char32) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: Writes one character, encoded as UTF-8.
doc.markdown:
Writes one character, encoded as UTF-8.
Reports `TextFailure(InvalidUtf8)` for a value that is not a Unicode scalar value. This is strict encoding, not
presentation: a caller that wants an invalid value shown as U+FFFD replaces it before calling.

params.name: scalar
params.markdown: the Unicode scalar value to encode and write

doc.returns: success when the encoded character was accepted
